chapter: Strings, arrangements and the Shrine band
title: School years and playing fiddle and trumpet at the tin roof dance job
summary: DeDroit graduated high school in 1910 and tells of his father's dance band and how he switched from fiddle to trumpet at a dance hall called the tin roof.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well, you'd say it was about in the teens, when they went, when they started getting more brass and reeds, and people just sort of, the others just sort of fell away? No, it was when I was going to high school,
and I graduated in 1910. About that time the Union insisted on a string with these five men.
Because of the fact that it was changing over at that time. It was changing over at that time. And

a case in point, I played it. Now, as I explained to you before, when I was going to school I wasn't waiting to study. You know what I'm saying? Mm-hmm. We had a dance job. My father had a dance job. My father was a band leader and a contract. And it was out of what we called a tin roof. There's a lot of difference between people as to what was the original tin roof. But I say it was on Washington Avenue. It was used for a prize fight arena. And they pushed the ring back and the band said, in the ring. And it was so big and had no acoustics. And I was the fiddler. But we happened to come off of a parade job. I don't know what it was. And I had my trumpet, but my fiddle. And the music was flat. So I took the bull by the horns and got my horn out and I played. And we didn't have any string but I had to fiddle in case somebody would. And then the people were satisfied with the music because I had more style and my father was strictly legit. He had a powerful lip and played well. But he couldn't interpolate an extra note. He wouldn't know. You see? So that's how I remember distinctly about the one string. On the old Robichaux arrangements, many of it are here. Well, he played left by the... He was a left-handed violinist, you know.
